outline: 1942 Permutations involving Grouping, Complements, and Cases

examples.question_text: A computer sends a sequence of $6$ binary digits. Each digit is $0$ or $1$. How many different sequences are possible?
examples.solution_text:
Each position has $2$ choices, including after earlier digits have been chosen.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}2\times2\times2\times2\times2\times2\\&=2^6\\&=64\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A serial code has $2$ English letters, followed by $3$ digits, followed by another English letter. Letters and digits may be repeated. Write the number of possible codes in index form.
examples.solution_text:
Use one box for each position.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}\text{Letter}&\text{Letter}&\text{Digit}&\text{Digit}&\text{Digit}&\text{Letter}\\26&26&10&10&10&26\end{array}$
Multiply the choices across all positions.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}26\times26\times10\times10\times10\times26\\&=26^3\times10^3\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A $5$-digit identification code starts with $62$. Each remaining position can contain any digit from $0$ to $9$, with repetition allowed. How many codes are possible?
examples.solution_text:
Each fixed digit has $1$ choice; each remaining position has $10$ choices.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}6&2&\text{Digit}&\text{Digit}&\text{Digit}\\1&1&10&10&10\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}1\times1\times10\times10\times10\\&=10^3\\&=1000\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A $3$-digit PIN uses only the odd digits $1,3,5,7,9$. Digits may be repeated. How many PINs are possible?
examples.solution_text:
There are $5$ permitted digits for each position.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}5\times5\times5\\&=5^3\\&=125\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Using the digits $1$ to $9$ with repetition allowed, how many $6$-digit numbers follow the pattern even-odd-even-odd-even-odd?
examples.solution_text:
There are $4$ even digits and $5$ odd digits.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}E&O&E&O&E&O\\4&5&4&5&4&5\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}4\times5\times4\times5\times4\times5\\&=4^3\times5^3\\&=8000\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A $5$-digit code uses digits $0$ to $9$, with repetition allowed. How many codes start and end with the same digit?
examples.solution_text:
Choose the first digit, then the three middle digits. The last digit is determined by the first.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}\text{First}&\text{Second}&\text{Third}&\text{Fourth}&\text{Last}\\10&10&10&10&1\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}10\times10\times10\times10\times1\\&=10^4\\&=10\,000\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Each sensor needs a different binary identification string. What is the minimum string length needed for $3000$ sensors?
examples.solution_text:
For a string of length $r$, there are $2^r$ possibilities. We need $2^r\geq3000$.
$\begin{align*}2^{11}&=2048<3000\\2^{12}&=4096\geq3000\end{align*}$
The minimum length is $12$ digits.

examples.question_text: A $6$-digit code starts with either $6$ or $7$. It contains no zero, and consecutive digits alternate between even and odd. Repetition is allowed. How many codes are possible?
examples.solution_text:
There are $4$ non-zero even digits and $5$ odd digits.

Case 1: starts with $6$. The pattern is E-O-E-O-E-O.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}1\times5\times4\times5\times4\times5\\&=5^3\times4^2\\&=2000\end{align*}$

Case 2: starts with $7$. The pattern is O-E-O-E-O-E.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}1\times4\times5\times4\times5\times4\\&=4^3\times5^2\\&=1600\end{align*}$

The cases are disjoint, so add their counts.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}2000+1600\\&=3600\end{align*}$

examples.derivation: Six distinguishable binary positions each have two choices: 2^6 = 64.
The six position counts are 26, 26, 10, 10, 10, 26. Their product is 26^3 × 10^3, matching the solution array.
The fixed prefix contributes 1 × 1 choices; three unrestricted digits contribute 10^3. Total: 1000.
Each of three positions admits five odd digits independently: 5^3 = 125.
Digits 1–9 provide four even and five odd choices. The specified six-position pattern gives 4 × 5 × 4 × 5 × 4 × 5 = 64 × 125 = 8000.
The first digit and three middle digits each have ten choices. The matching last digit has one conditional choice: 10^4 × 1 = 10,000.
2^11 = 2048 < 3000 and 2^12 = 4096 ≥ 3000. Since binary capacity increases with length, 12 digits is the minimum.
Starting with 6 gives 1 × 5 × 4 × 5 × 4 × 5 = 2000. Starting with 7 gives 1 × 4 × 5 × 4 × 5 × 4 = 1600. These disjoint cases exhaust the permitted starts, giving 3600.
